theme: The siege lifted; Elisha’s prophecies fulfilled
readingInstruction: Read 2 Kings 7:1-8:29. The siege of Samaria is lifted by four lepers, and Elisha’s prophecies are fulfilled. Notice how God’s word comes true in unexpected ways, and the quiet sadness of Elisha’s meeting with Hazael.
settingTheScene: Samaria is under siege by the Syrians, and the famine is so severe that people are eating the unthinkable. In the middle of the despair, Elisha announces that by tomorrow, food will be cheap. The chapter that follows tells how God does it. In chapter 8, the story widens to include the Shunammite woman’s land and the beginning of Hazael’s reign in Syria.
observation: Elisha says, “Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the LORD, Tomorrow about this time a seah of fine flour shall be sold for a shekel” (7:1).
The king’s officer says, “If the LORD himself should make windows in heaven, could this thing be?” (7:2).
Four lepers at the gate say, “Why are we sitting here until we die?” (7:3).
They find the Syrian camp abandoned: the LORD had made the army hear the sound of chariots and horses (7:6-7).
“We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news. If we are silent and wait until the morning light, punishment will overtake us. Now therefore come, let us go and tell” (7:9).
“And the people went out and plundered the camp of the Syrians” (7:16).
The officer who doubted is trampled at the gate and dies (7:17-20).
Elisha weeps before Hazael: “I know the evil that you will do to the people of Israel” (8:11-12).
interpretation:
The chapter turns on a surprising set of heroes. Four lepers, outcasts and untouchables, sitting outside the city gate, are the ones God uses to deliver Samaria. They have nothing to lose. They reason that if they stay, they die, and if they go to the Syrian camp, they may live. When they find the camp empty and full of food, they eat and hide treasure. Then their conscience speaks: “We are not doing right. This day is a day of good news.” They go to tell the city.

The scene is a picture of evangelism. The lepers did not earn the abundance. They were simply the first to discover it. Having received, they felt compelled to share. “This day is a day of good news.” The Greek word for gospel is “good news.” The image of beggars telling other beggars where to find bread is one that has been used to describe the gospel.

God’s word is fulfilled to the letter. The price of flour drops overnight, exactly as Elisha said. And the officer who scoffed, “Could this thing be?” sees it but does not eat of it. He is trampled in the rush at the gate. The word of the LORD does not fail, and unbelief has a cost.

In chapter 8, the story of the Shunammite’s land shows God’s providence in small things. She returns from famine exactly when the king is hearing Gehazi tell her story, and her land is restored. Timing is not an accident.

The meeting with Hazael is sobering. Elisha weeps when he sees what Hazael will do to Israel. Hazael, who calls himself a dog, will become a brutal king. Elisha does not rejoice in judgment. The prophet weeps over what God shows him. And the chapter ends with the continuing decline of Judah, which has now joined itself to Ahab’s family by marriage.
connection: The four lepers’ discovery is a picture of the gospel: poor, outcast people finding a feast and telling others. Jesus said, “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8). Jesus healed lepers (Luke 17:11-19) and sent his disciples to proclaim the good news. Elisha’s tears over Israel recall Jesus’ tears over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41). Hebrews 4:2 warns that the message did not benefit those who did not share the faith.
application:
Think of someone who needs to hear good news. Tell them today.

Examine yourself for unbelief like the officer’s, a “could this thing be?” attitude toward God’s word.

Weep over what grieves God, as Elisha did over Israel.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for good news for the poor, and ask him to make you someone who cannot keep it to yourself.
Confess where his word has met your unbelief.
Tell him one person to share it with.
